personality.blurb: Pairs usually stay together and come back to the same ledge year after year. Both parents feed their chicks a milk they make in their own throats.

origin: Wild rock doves nested on sea cliffs. People tamed them thousands of years ago, carried them everywhere, then let them go. To a pigeon, your building is a cliff.
home: The ledges are home. To a pigeon, a building ledge feels like the sea cliffs their ancestors nested on.

rightNow.spring: They're in the middle of courting season: males puffing up, turning round and round and bowing, while the females pretend not to notice.
rightNow.summer: They're raising chick after chick, taking turns on the eggs and barely pausing between families.
rightNow.fall: They're still nesting. City pigeons raise babies in any season, so some ledges near you have eggs on them right now.
rightNow.winter: They're huddling these days, fluffed into down jackets and pressed together on sunny ledges out of the wind.

funFact.title: Why you never see baby pigeons
funFact.body: They stay tucked in the nest until they're nearly grown. By the time you see one, they just look like a slightly scruffy adult.

kindness.title: Look at their feet.
kindness.body: String and hair get wrapped around pigeon toes and slowly cut off circulation. If you spot one, the Wild Bird Fund can help.

spotHint: Look up at building ledges, window air conditioners and the underside of train bridges.
withPeople: Pigeons can tell people apart by their faces, and in one study they remembered who had chased them, even after that person changed clothes. They've lived alongside humans for thousands of years, so mostly they treat us like part of the furniture.

personality.blurb: Sparrows do everything as a group: eat, bathe, argue, nap. The constant chirping is how they keep track of who's where.

origin: Brought over from England in the 1850s and let go in Brooklyn, in the hope they would eat caterpillars. They liked the city so much they spread across the whole continent.
home: The hedge is their clubhouse. They move as a group and chatter nonstop to keep track of each other.

rightNow.spring: They're stuffing messy nests into every gap they can find: signs, traffic lights, holes in old brick.
rightNow.summer: The block is full of fluffy young sparrows right now, following their parents around, wings fluttering, begging loudly.
rightNow.fall: They're dust-bathing by the curb on dry days and chattering in big gangs in the hedges.
rightNow.winter: They're tucked deep in the hedges together, puffed up into little round balls to stay warm.

funFact.title: They take baths in dirt
funFact.body: A sparrow wriggles into dry dust and flicks it through their feathers. It scrubs out oil and tiny bugs, like a dry shampoo.

kindness.title: Let the hedge grow shaggy.
kindness.body: A thick, untrimmed hedge is a safe place to hide from hawks and cold wind. If you can, wait until fall to trim.

spotHint: Listen for nonstop chirping coming from inside a hedge or bush.
withPeople: House sparrows have lived beside people for around ten thousand years and almost never nest far from buildings. They're bold at café tables but keep a careful eye on you the whole time.

personality.blurb: A squirrel can bury thousands of nuts in a fall, each in its own spot, and find many of them again months later by memory and smell.

origin: Gray squirrels are from here. The forests that once covered the city were their home, and in the 1800s people brought them back to the parks once trees were planted again.
home: The big tree is home base. They nest high up in a ball of leaves called a drey.

rightNow.spring: New babies are tucked in the drey, and the moms are dashing back and forth between feeding and keeping watch.
rightNow.summer: They're taking it easy. On hot days they flatten out on cool branches, legs spread, belly down.
rightNow.fall: They're burying nuts in every planter on the block. The ones they forget will be trees someday.
rightNow.winter: It's chase season: those wild loops around the tree trunks are squirrels courting.

funFact.title: They fake it when you're watching
funFact.body: If a squirrel thinks someone is watching, they may dig a hole, pretend to drop a nut, and cover up nothing at all. The real stash goes somewhere else.

kindness.title: Skip the junk food.
kindness.body: Bread, chips and candy fill them up without the nutrients they need. Unsalted nuts in the shell are a treat, now and then.

spotHint: Look for a ball of leaves high in a tree, and listen for scrabbling claws on bark.
withPeople: City squirrels are far more relaxed around people than country squirrels, and they learn quickly who carries snacks. They still keep a safe distance and an escape route up the nearest tree.

personality.blurb: Starlings pick up sounds from the world around them: other birds, whistles, even car alarms and phone ringtones, and mix them into their songs.

origin: About a hundred were let go in Central Park in 1890 and 1891. Today there are millions across North America, all from that one small group.
home: They hang out on the wire, chattering and doing impressions of car alarms.

rightNow.spring: They're dressed up in glossy purple and green with bright yellow beaks, singing from the rooftops to impress a mate.
rightNow.summer: Plain brown youngsters are out of the nest, following their parents across the lawns and begging.
rightNow.fall: They're gathering in big chattering groups on the wires at dusk before flying off to a shared roost.
rightNow.winter: They're wearing their winter coats: dark feathers covered in white speckles, like stars.

funFact.title: A murmuration is a dance
funFact.body: Thousands of starlings can swirl through the sky as one shape. Each bird is just watching their seven closest neighbors.

kindness.title: Wait to seal the gaps.
kindness.body: Starlings nest in holes in buildings. If you need to close one up, wait until the chicks have left in summer.

spotHint: Look along the wires at dusk for a row of chattering, shiny dark birds.
withPeople: Starlings keep their distance, but they're listening: they copy human sounds, from phone ringtones to car alarms, and slip them into their songs.

personality.blurb: Mourning doves sit close together on the wire, preening each other. That slow, sad hoo-oo-oo is actually a love song.

origin: They've always been here. Mourning doves are native birds who did well as forests turned into towns, fields and backyards.
home: That soft hooting at dawn is them, sitting side by side on the wire.

rightNow.spring: They're building the flimsiest nests you've ever seen: a few twigs on a fire escape, somehow enough.
rightNow.summer: They're raising family after family, one pair of squabs after another.
rightNow.fall: They're gathering in small groups to pick seeds off the ground in parks and yards.
rightNow.winter: They're sitting puffed up on sunny wires, soaking in every bit of warmth.

funFact.title: Their wings whistle
funFact.body: When a mourning dove takes off, their wings make a squeaky whistle. It may work as an alarm, telling others it's time to go.

kindness.title: Let the fire escape nest be.
kindness.body: If doves nest on your fire escape or planter, give them a few weeks of peace. The chicks leave in about two weeks.

spotHint: Listen at dawn for a soft, slow hoo-OO-oo-oo, then look for two plump birds on a wire.
withPeople: Doves are shy and flutter off when people get close, wings whistling. But they'll happily nest in a hanging planter or on a fire escape, right next to us.

personality.blurb: Robins are often the first voice of the dawn chorus. On the lawn they run, stop, tilt their head and pounce on a worm.

origin: Native all across North America. They were named by early settlers after the much smaller robin back in Europe, because of the orange chest.
home: They show up on the grass and sidewalk edges right after it rains.

rightNow.spring: They're singing before sunrise and sitting on sky-blue eggs in neat mud-lined cups.
rightNow.summer: Spotted-chest fledglings are hopping around on the ground while their parents bring them worms.
rightNow.fall: They're switching from worms to berries and gathering in loose flocks in the trees.
rightNow.winter: Many are staying all winter, quiet now, traveling in flocks and eating berries left on the trees.

funFact.title: That head tilt
funFact.body: A robin's eyes are on the sides of their head, so they tilt to look at the ground with one eye. Scientists think they may listen for worms too.

kindness.title: Skip lawn chemicals.
kindness.body: Robins eat what lives in the soil. A lawn without pesticides keeps the worms, and the robins, healthy.

spotHint: After a rain, check patches of grass for an orange-chested bird running and stopping.
withPeople: Robins are comfortable on lawns near people and will follow someone digging in a garden, waiting for the worms to turn up.

personality.blurb: Gulls figure things out. They drop clams onto hard ground to crack them, and they watch people very closely for snacks.

origin: Native coastal birds. New York's rivers, harbor and beaches have always had gulls, and rooftops make good stand-in cliffs.
home: Always overhead, always riding the wind off the river.

rightNow.spring: They're nesting on flat rooftops and harbor islands and loudly defending their spot.
rightNow.summer: Mottled brown youngsters are out, following their parents and whining for food.
rightNow.fall: More gulls are arriving along the waterfront every week as the cooler air brings them in from the north.
rightNow.winter: There are more gulls around now than any other season, standing in big mixed groups on the ice and the piers.

funFact.title: The red spot is a doorbell
funFact.body: Adult herring gulls have a red spot on their beak. Chicks peck at it, and that tells the parent to bring up food.

kindness.title: Pick up fishing line.
kindness.body: Lost fishing line tangles gulls' legs and wings. If you see some on the pier or beach, put it in the trash.

spotHint: Look up near the water or over parking lots for big white-and-gray birds gliding.
withPeople: Gulls watch what we eat. In one study, gulls took much longer to go for a bag of chips when a person was looking right at them. A steady stare helps protect a sandwich.

personality.blurb: Raccoons feel the world through their front paws, which are super sensitive. They remember routes and solutions, and use them night after night.

origin: Native to North America. They lived in the forests here long before the city, and adapted to it better than almost anyone.
home: The night shift. You know where to find them.

rightNow.spring: Babies are being born in hidden dens in tree holes and old buildings, and the moms are out foraging even by day to keep up.
rightNow.summer: Moms are leading lines of youngsters on their first rounds of the neighborhood.
rightNow.fall: They're eating everything they can find to build up fat for winter.
rightNow.winter: They're spending the coldest nights curled up in the den, sometimes for days at a time.

funFact.title: Daytime doesn't mean sick
funFact.body: A raccoon out in daylight is usually just a busy mom or a hungry youngster. Give them space. If one is stumbling, circling or acting strange, keep away and call 311 in NYC or Animal Control in Jersey City.

kindness.title: Put a lid on it.
kindness.body: A trash can with a tight lid keeps raccoons safe from sharp edges, spoiled food and run-ins with people.

spotHint: After dark, look along fences and near trash cans for a masked face.
withPeople: City raccoons are bolder than country ones and have learned to open latches, lids and bins. They're curious about us but wild, and it's best for everyone when we don't feed them.

personality.blurb: The monarchs passing through in fall will fly all the way to the mountains of Mexico, a place none of them has ever been.

origin: Native to the Americas. Every fall, monarchs from the East head to the same forests in central Mexico, and their great-grandchildren come back north.
home: Just passing through, stopping at every flower box on the way.

rightNow.spring: They're working their way north, generation by generation. The first ones are just reaching the city.
rightNow.summer: They're laying eggs on milkweed, the only plant their caterpillars can eat.
rightNow.fall: They're passing through on the way to Mexico, stopping to drink from the late flowers.
rightNow.winter: Right now they're far away in Mexico, clustered by the millions on fir trees in the mountains.

funFact.title: Poison is their armor
funFact.body: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and keep its bitter chemicals in their bodies. Birds learn fast that orange-and-black tastes awful.

kindness.title: Plant milkweed.
kindness.body: A pot of native milkweed on a stoop or fire escape gives monarchs a place to lay eggs. Late flowers fuel their trip south.

spotHint: In late summer and fall, watch flower boxes and park gardens for a big orange butterfly gliding.
withPeople: Monarchs don't mind people at all, and people love them back: every fall, volunteers put tiny stickers on their wings to track the trip to Mexico.

personality.blurb: A red-tail can sit on a ledge for an hour without moving, watching the ground below for a rat to step out.

origin: Native and common across North America. They've moved into the city, nesting on buildings and hunting the rats and pigeons here.
home: Up on the rooftops and light poles, watching the street below.

rightNow.spring: They're sitting on eggs in big stick nests on building ledges and in tall trees.
rightNow.summer: Young hawks are learning to hunt, and screaming for their parents while they figure it out.
rightNow.fall: Hawks from the north are streaming over the city on their way south, while the locals stay put.
rightNow.winter: They're courting: pairs soar together and sometimes lock talons in the air.

funFact.title: That movie eagle is a hawk
funFact.body: The fierce scream you hear when an eagle appears in a movie is usually a red-tailed hawk. Real bald eagles sound more like giggles.

kindness.title: Give them room to eat.
kindness.body: If a hawk lands on the ground with a meal, stop and watch from a distance. Crowding them can make them drop dinner and fly off hungry.

spotHint: Look up at rooftop edges and light poles for a big bird sitting very still.
withPeople: Red-tailed hawks have made themselves at home in the city, nesting on building ledges above busy avenues. They tolerate people below them, as long as nobody gets too close.

personality.blurb: Jays bury acorns all over, and the ones they forget grow into oak trees. They also copy hawk calls, maybe to clear everyone else away.

origin: Native to eastern North America, at home anywhere there are tall trees and acorns.
home: Up in the treetops, announcing everything that happens below.

rightNow.spring: They've gone unusually quiet, slipping in and out of their nests without a sound.
rightNow.summer: Families are traveling together through the trees, the young ones copying everything.
rightNow.fall: They're burying acorns all over, and some are flying south in loose flocks along the coast.
rightNow.winter: They're bright blue against the bare branches, and loud about it.

funFact.title: They aren't really blue
funFact.body: There's no blue color in a blue jay's feathers. Tiny structures inside scatter light so they look blue. Crush a feather and it turns brown.

kindness.title: Keep an oak in mind.
kindness.body: If your block has room for a new tree, ask for an oak. One oak feeds jays, squirrels and hundreds of kinds of insects.

spotHint: Listen for a loud, bossy JAY! JAY! from the treetops.
withPeople: Blue jays notice everything, people included, and will sound the alarm when someone walks by. They learn quickly where the feeders are, and who fills them.

personality.blurb: Juncos spend summer in northern forests and come down for the winter. When they fly off, white feathers flash on both sides of the tail.

origin: Native birds of North America. They breed in Canada and the mountains, and spend the cold months here.
home: Hopping under the hedge, picking at seeds on the ground.

rightNow.spring: They're getting ready to head north, trilling before they go.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're far up north in the forests of Canada, raising chicks.
rightNow.fall: They're just arriving from Canada: little gray birds hopping under the bushes.
rightNow.winter: They're settled in for the season, hopping around in small flocks under the hedges.

funFact.title: Why people call them snowbirds
funFact.body: They tend to show up just as the weather turns cold, and they look like they're wearing a dark gray sky over a snowy belly.

kindness.title: Leave the leaves.
kindness.body: Juncos scratch through leaf litter for seeds and bugs. A leafy corner under a bush is their favorite diner.

spotHint: From October to April, look under hedges for small slate-gray birds with white bellies.
withPeople: Juncos are shy around people and stay close to the safety of a hedge, flashing their white tail feathers as they dart back in.

personality.blurb: Opossums wander at night, eating slugs, beetles, fallen fruit and scraps. When very scared, they faint without meaning to, and wake up when it's safe.

origin: North America's only marsupial, carrying babies in a pouch like a kangaroo. Their family has been around since the time of the dinosaurs.
home: Moving along the fence at night, quiet and in no hurry.

rightNow.spring: The moms are carrying tiny babies in their pouches, sometimes more than a dozen.
rightNow.summer: Young opossums are heading off on their own, exploring yards and alleys for the first time.
rightNow.fall: They're bulking up on fallen fruit and bugs before the cold.
rightNow.winter: It's a hard season, so on cold nights they're staying in the den to protect their bare ears and tails.

funFact.title: Rabies is rare for them
funFact.body: Opossums have a low body temperature, which makes it hard for the rabies virus to survive. They hiss to look scary, but they're mostly bluffing.

kindness.title: Check the pouch.
kindness.body: If you find an opossum hit by a car, there may be living babies in the pouch. Call a wildlife rehabber right away.

spotHint: After dark, look along fences and back alleys for a white face and a long bare tail.
withPeople: Opossums would rather avoid us entirely. When they're truly terrified they faint, without meaning to, and wake up once things are calm.

personality.blurb: Crows recognize individual people and remember how they were treated. Families stick together, and last year's kids help raise the new chicks.

origin: Native across North America. Crows have lived alongside people for thousands of years, learning our routines.
home: Up on the rooftops, keeping an eye on everything.

rightNow.spring: They're nesting high in the trees, with older siblings helping bring food to the new chicks.
rightNow.summer: Noisy families with begging youngsters are moving through the neighborhood together.
rightNow.fall: Families are joining up into bigger groups and flying to shared roosts at dusk.
rightNow.winter: They're sleeping in huge roosts with thousands of other crows, spreading out over the city every morning.

funFact.title: Why it's called a murder
funFact.body: The name is an old, spooky bit of English wordplay. Crows are actually caring family birds who even gather around a crow who has died.

kindness.title: Be a friendly face.
kindness.body: Crows remember people. Be calm and kind around them, and you may find yourself with neighbors who nod back.

spotHint: Listen for a loud caw-caw from the rooftops, then look for big all-black birds.
withPeople: Crows remember human faces for years, and they tell each other about people who bothered them, so a whole flock may scold someone who's never met them. They remember kind people too.

personality.blurb: Their thin whistled song sounds like Oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada. Some have white head stripes and some have tan ones.

origin: Native birds who raise their families in the forests of Canada and spend the winter in parks and backyards down here.
home: In the bushes and leaf litter, scratching with both feet at once.

rightNow.spring: They're singing their whistled song before heading back to Canada.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're up north in Canadian forests, raising chicks on the forest floor.
rightNow.fall: They've just arrived for the winter. Listen for their thin whistled song in the bushes.
rightNow.winter: They're scratching through the leaves in small groups, kicking backward with both feet.

funFact.title: Two kinds, one bird
funFact.body: White-striped and tan-striped birds are the same species, and they almost always pair up with the other style.

kindness.title: Turn off the lights.
kindness.body: They migrate at night, and bright city lights pull them off course into windows. Lights out on big migration nights helps.

spotHint: From October to May, listen for a thin whistled song from low bushes in parks.
withPeople: White-throats are shy and stick close to the shrubs, but if you stand still in a park in winter, they'll go right back to scratching in the leaves near your feet.

personality.blurb: Swifts eat, drink and even bathe while flying. Their feet can't grip a branch, so when they rest, they cling to the inside of a chimney.

origin: Native birds who once roosted in hollow trees. When forests were cut down, they moved into chimneys instead.
home: Zipping over the rooftops, twittering, all summer long.

rightNow.spring: They're just back from South America, twittering overhead.
rightNow.summer: They're zipping over the rooftops catching bugs, and nesting inside old chimneys.
rightNow.fall: They've gone south. Before they left, hundreds swirled into big chimneys at dusk.
rightNow.winter: Right now they're far away in the Amazon, catching bugs over the rainforest.

funFact.title: Glued-on nests
funFact.body: A chimney swift builds their nest out of twigs and glues it to the chimney wall with their own sticky spit.

kindness.title: Leave old chimneys open.
kindness.body: If a building has an unused chimney, keeping it uncapped from spring to fall gives swifts a place to nest.

spotHint: From late April to September, look up for tiny cigar-shaped birds zipping and twittering.
withPeople: Chimney swifts depend on us now: with few big hollow trees left, they nest and sleep almost entirely in human chimneys.

personality.blurb: While bees sleep, moths visit flowers at night and spread their pollen. Many are as colorful as butterflies up close.

origin: There are many kinds of moths in the city, most of them native. They are older than butterflies, which actually evolved from moths.
home: Circling the streetlight after dark.

rightNow.spring: They're coming out of their cocoons as the nights get warmer.
rightNow.summer: It's peak moth season: hundreds of kinds are flying on warm nights.
rightNow.fall: The last ones are flying, and many are already tucked into fallen leaves as cocoons.
rightNow.winter: Most are asleep as eggs and cocoons, though a few winter moths are flying on mild nights.

funFact.title: Why they circle lights
funFact.body: Moths keep their back to the brightest thing in the sky to know which way is up. A streetlight tricks them into flying in circles.

kindness.title: Switch off the porch light.
kindness.body: Every outdoor light you turn off at night saves moths from circling until they're worn out.

spotHint: On a warm night, look at the glow around a streetlight or porch light.
withPeople: Moths aren't interested in us, but our lights trap them, circling until they're exhausted. Turning off outdoor lights is the biggest favor we can do them.

personality.blurb: Canada Geese pair up for life and raise their goslings together, one parent grazing while the other keeps watch. Get too close and you'll hear a very clear hiss.

origin: Native to North America. Many Canada Geese in the city don't migrate at all anymore. They stay all year wherever the grass is good.
home: Grazing the lawns by the water and floating in pairs on the pond.

rightNow.spring: Goslings are hatching, and both parents are walking them to the water and hissing at anyone who gets too close.
rightNow.summer: They're molting and can't fly for a few weeks, so they're staying close to the water and keeping a low profile.
rightNow.fall: Flocks from the north are passing over in big honking Vs while the locals settle in.
rightNow.winter: They're gathered on open water and grassy edges, standing on one foot to keep the other warm.

funFact.title: Taking turns at the front
funFact.body: Geese fly in a V so each bird gets a little lift from the one ahead. They take turns doing the hard work at the front.

kindness.title: Skip the bread.
kindness.body: Bread fills geese up without feeding them. Let them graze the grass and water plants their bodies actually need.

spotHint: Look on big lawns near water for brown-and-black birds with a white chinstrap.
withPeople: Geese are relaxed in busy parks, but in spring they defend nests and goslings with hissing and spread wings. That's a request for space, not an attack.

personality.blurb: Mallards feed by tipping forward with their tails in the air. That loud QUACK? Almost always a female. Males make a softer, raspy sound.

origin: Native across the Northern Hemisphere, and the wild ancestor of almost every farm duck.
home: Paddling on the pond, tipping bottoms-up to snack on water plants.

rightNow.spring: There are ducklings! Moms are leading lines of fluffy ducklings around the pond, all on their own.
rightNow.summer: The males are in their brown "eclipse" feathers, looking like the females while new feathers grow in.
rightNow.fall: Pairs are forming: the males have their shiny green heads back and are showing off on the water.
rightNow.winter: They're staying as long as there's open water, dabbling along the edges of the ice.

funFact.title: Built-in raincoat
funFact.body: Mallards spread oil from a gland near their tail all over their feathers, so water rolls right off.

kindness.title: Give the ducklings space.
kindness.body: Keep dogs leashed near the pond in spring. A duckling who gets separated from mom has a hard time on their own.

spotHint: Check the edges of any pond for ducks tipping bottoms-up. The males have shiny green heads.
withPeople: Mallards are at ease around people and will paddle right up. Bread fills them up without feeding them, so the kindest thing is to just enjoy the visit.

personality.blurb: Brant raise their families in the high Arctic and fly thousands of miles to spend the winter in New York Harbor, grazing sea lettuce and waterfront lawns.

origin: Native sea geese who nest on the Arctic tundra and spend the winter along the Atlantic coast.
home: Grazing the grassy edge by the water, or bobbing in a flock close to shore.

rightNow.spring: They're fueling up on sea lettuce before flying back to the Arctic.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're far north on the Arctic tundra, raising goslings under the midnight sun.
rightNow.fall: They're just arriving from the Arctic. Listen for their low, rolling cronk along the shore.
rightNow.winter: Big flocks are grazing waterfront lawns and bobbing in the harbor, chattering away.

funFact.title: Salt-water geese
funFact.body: Brant spend most of their lives on salt water and can drink it, thanks to special glands that get rid of the salt.

kindness.title: Let them graze in peace.
kindness.body: Brant need every bite to fuel their trip back to the Arctic. Walk around a grazing flock instead of through it.

spotHint: From fall to spring, look along the shore for small dark geese with a white necklace.
withPeople: Brant are wary and lift off together if someone walks too close, but they've learned to graze on ballfields and lawns by the water, near people.

personality.blurb: Cormorants chase fish underwater, then stand on a post with their wings spread wide to dry. Their feathers soak up a little water, which actually helps them dive.

origin: Native birds who nest in big colonies on the islands of New York Harbor.
home: Standing on an old piling with wings spread wide, drying off.

rightNow.spring: They're back on the harbor islands, building messy stick nests in big, noisy colonies.
rightNow.summer: They're busy feeding chicks, diving for fish all day and drying off on every post in the harbor.
rightNow.fall: Long lines of them are flying south, low over the water.
rightNow.winter: Most are down south, though a few tough ones are still fishing the harbor.

funFact.title: Why the wing pose
funFact.body: Cormorant feathers aren't fully waterproof. That makes them heavier and better at diving, but it means they have to stand and dry off.

kindness.title: Pick up fishing line.
kindness.body: Cormorants dive after fish and can get tangled in lost line and hooks. Bin any you find by the water.

spotHint: Look at posts and pilings in the water for a dark bird standing with wings held out.
withPeople: Cormorants keep their distance from people and fly off if you get close to their piling. From a respectful spot, you can watch them dry their wings for a long time.

personality.blurb: Smaller and neater than herring gulls, ring-billed gulls are as at home on a ballfield or a parking lot as on the beach.

origin: Native birds who nest around the Great Lakes and in Canada and spend the cooler months here.
home: Standing around the shore and open lawns, keeping an eye on everything.

rightNow.spring: Most are heading north to nest by the Great Lakes, but a few are staying behind.
rightNow.summer: There are fewer around, mostly young gulls who aren't nesting yet.
rightNow.fall: They're arriving back in big numbers, filling the shore, the ballfields and the parking lots.
rightNow.winter: They're everywhere: on the piers, on the ice and on every open lawn near the water.

funFact.title: Read the ring
funFact.body: That neat black ring near the tip of the yellow beak is how you tell them apart from the bigger herring gulls.

kindness.title: Don't share your fries.
kindness.body: Salty, greasy food isn't good for gulls, and feeding them teaches them to crowd people. Let them find their own lunch.

spotHint: Look for neat white-and-gray gulls with a black ring around a yellow beak.
withPeople: Ring-billed gulls are completely at home in parking lots, ballfields and beaches, anywhere people drop a fry or two.

personality.blurb: Terns hover over the water, then plunge headfirst after small fish. Near their nests they'll swoop at anyone who wanders too close.

origin: Native seabirds who nest on beaches and islands around the harbor and spend the winter in South America.
home: Hovering over the water, then splash, diving for a fish.

rightNow.spring: They're back from South America and courting with gifts of fish.
rightNow.summer: They're raising chicks on harbor islands and beaches, diving for tiny fish all day long.
rightNow.fall: They're heading south to spend the winter in South America.
rightNow.winter: Right now they're far away on the coasts of South America.

funFact.title: Fish for a date
funFact.body: A male tern courts by flying around with a small fish in his beak, then offering it to the female.

kindness.title: Give nesting beaches room.
kindness.body: Terns nest right on the sand. Stay out of roped-off beach areas in summer so the eggs and chicks stay safe.

spotHint: In summer, watch over the water for slim white birds with black caps who hover, then dive.
withPeople: Terns are gentle with people until you walk near their nests. Then they dive at your head, calling loudly, until you move along.

personality.blurb: A great blue heron can stand motionless in the shallows for ages, then strike at a fish faster than you can blink.

origin: Native across North America, nesting together in tree colonies called rookeries.
home: Standing still at the water's edge, tall among the reeds.

rightNow.spring: They're nesting high in trees on the harbor islands, adding sticks to big old nests.
rightNow.summer: They're fishing the shallows of every pond and shore to feed hungry chicks.
rightNow.fall: Young herons are out on their own, trying out fishing spots all over the city.
rightNow.winter: Some are staying all winter, hunched by the open water, waiting for a fish.

funFact.title: The folded neck
funFact.body: Herons fly with their necks folded into an S. Cranes fly with their necks stretched straight out.

kindness.title: Watch from a distance.
kindness.body: A heron who flies off loses energy and a good fishing spot. Stop, enjoy, and let them keep fishing.

spotHint: Scan the edges of ponds and shores for a tall gray-blue bird standing perfectly still.
withPeople: Herons are wary and lift off with a croak if people come too close, but some city herons get used to joggers on the path and keep fishing.

personality.blurb: Black-crowned night herons nap in the trees by day and fish at dusk and through the night, hunched at the water's edge.

origin: Native herons who nest in colonies on the harbor islands and roost in the trees around city ponds.
home: Hunched on the rocks at the water's edge, waiting for dusk.

rightNow.spring: They're back at their nesting colonies, crowded into the trees on the harbor islands.
rightNow.summer: They're fishing the ponds and shores at dusk and through the night.
rightNow.fall: Young night herons, brown with white spots, are exploring new fishing spots.
rightNow.winter: Most have gone south, but a few are roosting in evergreens near open water.

funFact.title: Built for the dark
funFact.body: Those big red eyes help night herons see in low light, so they can fish while most herons are asleep.

kindness.title: Let the roost rest.
kindness.body: By day they sleep in trees near water. Keep your voice low near a roost so they're rested for the night shift.

spotHint: At dusk, look along the water's edge for a stocky, hunched bird with a black cap and red eyes.
withPeople: Night herons often sleep in trees right over busy park paths, hunched and still, while people walk underneath without noticing.

personality.blurb: One of the smallest ducks around, buffleheads dive over and over, popping back up somewhere you didn't expect.

origin: Native ducks who nest in old woodpecker holes in northern forests and spend the winter on our bays and rivers.
home: Diving and popping up again out on the water.

rightNow.spring: They're heading north to the forests of Canada to nest in old woodpecker holes.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're far north, raising ducklings in tree holes by forest lakes.
rightNow.fall: They're just arriving on the harbor and rivers for the winter.
rightNow.winter: Small flocks are diving all day out on the water, white head patches flashing.

funFact.title: Nests in a tree
funFact.body: Buffleheads nest in old woodpecker holes. The ducklings jump down to the ground the day after they hatch.

kindness.title: Keep the water clean.
kindness.body: Diving ducks swallow what they find. Trash and fishing line in the water are real hazards for them.

spotHint: In winter, look out on the water for tiny black-and-white ducks who keep diving.
withPeople: Buffleheads are shy and stay out on the water, diving away from boats and people. Binoculars are the best way to say hello.

personality.blurb: Mute swans hiss, snort and whoosh their wings loudly. Pairs stay together for years and defend their nest and cygnets fiercely.

origin: Brought over from Europe in the 1800s to decorate parks and estates. Today they live wild on our ponds and bays.
home: Gliding on the pond, neck curved in a graceful S.

rightNow.spring: They're sitting on huge nests at the pond's edge. Give them lots of room: they're very protective right now.
rightNow.summer: Fluffy gray cygnets are paddling behind their parents, sometimes riding on their backs.
rightNow.fall: The cygnets are growing up, still gray-brown, still following their parents around.
rightNow.winter: They're gathered on open water, sometimes in big groups when the ponds freeze.

funFact.title: Listen to the wings
funFact.body: You can hear a flying mute swan coming: their wings make a loud, rhythmic whooshing hum.

kindness.title: Admire from a distance.
kindness.body: Swans defending a nest will hiss and charge. Keep back, keep dogs leashed, and everyone stays calm.

spotHint: Look on ponds and quiet bays for a big white bird with an orange beak and an S-curved neck.
withPeople: Swans are calm most of the year, but near their nest a swan will raise their wings and charge. Give them lots of room in spring.

personality.blurb: Male red-winged blackbirds puff up their red-and-yellow shoulders and belt out conk-la-ree! from the tops of the cattails.

origin: Native across North America and one of the most common birds on the continent, at home in any marsh.
home: Clinging to the top of a cattail, singing his heart out.

rightNow.spring: They're among the first birds back, the males claiming their cattails and singing.
rightNow.summer: They're feeding chicks in the reeds and chasing off anyone who flies too close to the nest.
rightNow.fall: They're gathering in big flocks with grackles and starlings before heading south.
rightNow.winter: Most have gone south, but a few tough ones are sticking around the marshes.

funFact.title: The brown ones are the girls
funFact.body: Female red-winged blackbirds are streaky brown and look like big sparrows. They do most of the nest building.

kindness.title: Leave the wild edges.
kindness.body: Cattails and reeds by ponds are their home. Leaving those edges uncut gives them somewhere to nest.

spotHint: Near ponds in spring and summer, listen for conk-la-ree! and look for a black bird with red shoulders on a cattail.
withPeople: Red-wings are fine with people most of the year, but in spring a male may dive at your head if you walk too close to the nest.

personality.blurb: Deer slip through the trees at dawn and dusk. When something startles them, they flip up their white tails like a flag and bound away.

origin: Native to North America. In the city they live mostly on Staten Island, where they came back in the last few decades, swimming over from New Jersey. They slip through wooded edges and parks across the island, and across the harbor a small herd lives in the wild, fenced-off middle of Liberty State Park.
home: Stepping quietly through the edge of the woods at dawn and dusk.

rightNow.spring: The moms are looking for quiet spots in tall grass. Spotted fawns are on the way.
rightNow.summer: Spotted fawns are lying hidden in the grass while their moms feed nearby. A fawn alone is usually just fine.
rightNow.fall: The bucks have their antlers, and everyone is bulking up on acorns before winter.
rightNow.winter: They're gathered in small groups, nibbling twigs and staying close to shelter.

funFact.title: Fawns hide by staying still
funFact.body: Newborn fawns have very little scent, so mom leaves them tucked away and motionless while she feeds, then comes back to nurse.

kindness.title: Leave the fawn.
kindness.body: A fawn alone in the grass hasn't been abandoned. Mom is nearby. Look, smile, and walk away quietly.

spotHint: At dawn or dusk, look along the wooded edges of big parks for a brown deer with a white-flagged tail.
withPeople: Deer avoid people and freeze or bound away when startled. Where they live near neighborhoods, they get used to the sights and sounds of people, but they stay wild.

personality.blurb: Mockingbirds learn the songs of other birds (and car alarms, and squeaky gates) and string them together for minutes at a time. Some sing right through the night.

origin: Native birds who moved north into New York over the last century as yards, parks and berry bushes spread.
home: Up on the highest antenna, chimney or treetop, singing everything they know.

rightNow.spring: They're singing nonstop, sometimes all night, to win over a mate.
rightNow.summer: They're guarding their nests and chasing off cats, crows and anyone else who gets too close.
rightNow.fall: They're claiming berry bushes for the winter and defending them fiercely.
rightNow.winter: They're quieter now, but still guarding their favorite berry bush from every other bird.

funFact.title: Hundreds of songs
funFact.body: A single mockingbird can learn up to around 200 different songs, including other birds, frogs and car alarms.

kindness.title: Keep the berry bushes.
kindness.body: Winterberry, holly and other berry shrubs feed mockingbirds through the cold months. Leave the berries on.

spotHint: Listen for a long string of different songs from a rooftop antenna or treetop, then look for a slim gray bird.
withPeople: Mockingbirds remember people who come near their nest, and in one study they flew at those same people again days later, while ignoring strangers.

personality.blurb: Cardinal couples stay together all year. In spring the male feeds the female seed by seed, beak to beak, like a little kiss.

origin: Native birds who spread north into New York over the last hundred years, following backyards and bird feeders.
home: Tucked in the thickest part of the hedge, flashing red.

rightNow.spring: The males are feeding their partners beak to beak, and the pairs are singing back and forth.
rightNow.summer: They're raising chicks in dense shrubs, sometimes two or three families a summer.
rightNow.fall: Pairs are sticking close together, snacking on seeds and berries.
rightNow.winter: They're bright red against the snow, puffed up round, visiting the same hedges every day.

funFact.title: The girls sing too
funFact.body: Female cardinals sing, often from the nest, possibly to tell their partner what they need.

kindness.title: Leave some shrubs thick.
kindness.body: Cardinals nest and hide in dense bushes. A shaggy hedge is a five-star hotel for them.

spotHint: Look for a flash of bright red in a hedge, or listen for a loud, clear whistle: cheer, cheer, cheer.
withPeople: Cardinals are a little shy but happily visit feeders and yards. They sometimes attack their own reflection in a window or car mirror, thinking it's a rival.

personality.blurb: Grackles strut across lawns with their long tails held in a V. Their song sounds like a rusty gate, and they're proud of it.

origin: Native blackbirds of eastern North America who love open lawns with a few tall trees.
home: Strutting across the sidewalk and lawn, tail held in a V.

rightNow.spring: They're back in force, males puffing up and squeaking their rusty-gate songs from the treetops.
rightNow.summer: They're walking the lawns with beaks full of bugs for their chicks.
rightNow.fall: They're gathering in huge noisy flocks with other blackbirds before heading south.
rightNow.winter: Most have gone south, and a few are hanging around with the starlings.

funFact.title: Shiny in the sun
funFact.body: Grackles look black until the light hits them. Then their heads shine purple-blue and their bodies glow bronze.

kindness.title: Let the lawn get a little wild.
kindness.body: Grackles find their bugs in lawns without pesticides. A few dandelions are a feast.

spotHint: Look on lawns for a long-tailed black bird with bright yellow eyes, strutting.
withPeople: Grackles are bold around people, strutting between café tables and dunking found crackers in puddles to soften them.

personality.blurb: Catbirds hide in thick bushes and make a call that sounds exactly like a cat's meow. Then they launch into a long, rambling song.

origin: Native songbirds who spend summer in our thickets and winter in the southern US and the Caribbean.
home: Hidden deep in the shrubs, meowing.

rightNow.spring: They're just back from the south, singing long rambling songs from inside the bushes.
rightNow.summer: They're raising chicks in dense thickets and gobbling berries.
rightNow.fall: They're fattening up on berries before heading south.
rightNow.winter: Right now they're down south, in the Gulf states, Central America and the Caribbean.

funFact.title: Two voices at once
funFact.body: Catbirds, like other mimics, can sing two notes at the same time, one from each side of their voice box.

kindness.title: Plant native berries.
kindness.body: Serviceberry, elderberry and dogwood fuel catbirds for their migration.

spotHint: Listen for a meow from a thick bush, then look for a slim gray bird with a black cap.
withPeople: Catbirds are curious and will often pop out of a bush to see who's there, meowing at you.

personality.blurb: Song sparrows sing on bright days even in winter. Each male knows several songs, and neighbors often match each other.

origin: Native sparrows found almost everywhere in North America, from marsh edges to backyard hedges.
home: Perched on a shrub by the water's edge, singing.

rightNow.spring: They're singing from the top of every shrub to claim a spot.
rightNow.summer: They're raising one family after another in low, hidden nests.
rightNow.fall: More are arriving from the north, filling the weedy edges and hedges.
rightNow.winter: They're still here, and still singing on sunny days.

funFact.title: Learning from the neighbors
funFact.body: Young song sparrows learn their songs from the males around them, so each neighborhood has its own local tunes.

kindness.title: Leave weedy edges.
kindness.body: Seed heads and tangles along fences and water feed song sparrows all winter.

spotHint: Look for a streaky brown sparrow with a dark spot in the middle of their chest, singing from a low shrub.
withPeople: Song sparrows are used to people walking by their shrubs and keep singing anyway, a little soundtrack for anyone near the water.

personality.blurb: Kestrels are falcons about the size of a mourning dove. They hover in midair over a lawn, then drop down onto a grasshopper.

origin: Native falcons who nest in cavities, including nooks in old city buildings.
home: Hovering over the open sky above the street, wings fluttering.

rightNow.spring: Pairs are checking out nooks in old buildings for a nest.
rightNow.summer: The parents are hunting grasshoppers and mice for their chicks.
rightNow.fall: Migrating kestrels are streaming past along the coast.
rightNow.winter: Some are staying all winter, perched on wires and light poles, watching the ground.

funFact.title: They see invisible trails
funFact.body: Kestrels can see ultraviolet light. Experiments with their European cousins suggest it might help them spot the trails voles leave behind, though scientists still debate how much.

kindness.title: Skip the pesticides.
kindness.body: Kestrels eat grasshoppers and other bugs. Lawns without pesticides keep their food safe.

spotHint: Look for a small, colorful falcon hovering in place over a lawn or perched on a wire.
withPeople: Kestrels are wary of people, and their numbers have dropped. People help by putting up nest boxes, which kestrels readily move into.

personality.blurb: Cooper's hawks dart through trees and around corners at top speed, chasing small birds. They're built for twists and turns.

origin: Native hawks who have moved into cities in a big way over recent decades.
home: Hidden high in a tree, watching.

rightNow.spring: Pairs are building nests high in trees in parks and yards.
rightNow.summer: The parents are bringing food to fluffy white chicks.
rightNow.fall: Young hawks are learning to hunt, and migrants are passing through.
rightNow.winter: They're patrolling the neighborhood, sometimes sitting very still near busy bird spots.

funFact.title: Built for tight turns
funFact.body: Their short rounded wings and long tail let Cooper's hawks steer through branches like a fighter jet.

kindness.title: Make windows visible.
kindness.body: Hawks chasing birds can crash into glass too. Window decals help everyone.

spotHint: Watch for a crow-sized hawk with a long striped tail darting through trees.
withPeople: Cooper's hawks have learned that backyard bird feeders are good hunting spots, and they're surprisingly at ease in busy neighborhoods.

personality.blurb: Peregrines dive after pigeons at over 200 miles an hour, making them the fastest animal on Earth. City bridges and skyscrapers make perfect cliffs for them.

origin: Native falcons who nearly disappeared in the 1960s because of the pesticide DDT, and came back. New York City now has one of the highest densities of nesting peregrines anywhere.
home: Perched high on a ledge or bridge tower, scanning the sky.

rightNow.spring: They're nesting on bridges and skyscraper ledges, with eggs in a scrape on bare stone.
rightNow.summer: Young peregrines are learning to fly and practicing dives over the rooftops.
rightNow.fall: Migrating peregrines are passing down the coast, while the city pairs stay.
rightNow.winter: Pairs are back at their favorite ledges, perched together on cold, bright days.

funFact.title: Over 200 miles an hour
funFact.body: In a hunting dive, called a stoop, a peregrine can top 200 miles per hour.

kindness.title: Watch from far away.
kindness.body: Peregrine nests on bridges and tall buildings are protected. Enjoy them from the street or through binoculars, and give them their sky.

spotHint: Look up at bridge towers and tall ledges for a sleek falcon with a dark helmet.
withPeople: Peregrines nest on bridges and skyscrapers, and people help them along: city wildlife staff watch over the nests and band the chicks every year.

personality.blurb: Downy woodpeckers are tiny and busy, hitching up tree trunks and tapping for bugs. In spring they drum fast rhythms on hollow branches to talk to each other.

origin: Native woodpeckers found in almost every park and leafy street with big trees.
home: Clinging to a tree trunk, tapping for bugs.

rightNow.spring: They're drumming fast rhythms on hollow branches to call to a mate.
rightNow.summer: They're feeding chicks in a hole they carved in a dead branch.
rightNow.fall: They're picking insects out of bark and joining flocks with chickadees and titmice.
rightNow.winter: They're tapping through the cold and tucking into a tree hole each night.

funFact.title: A tongue that wraps around their head
funFact.body: When it's tucked away, a woodpecker's long tongue wraps around the back of their skull. Strong neck muscles power all that pecking.

kindness.title: Leave dead branches.
kindness.body: Dead wood is full of bugs and good nest holes. If it's safe, let an old branch stay.

spotHint: Listen for soft tapping and look for a small black-and-white bird hitching up a trunk.
withPeople: Downies are easygoing around people and visit backyard suet feeders, hopping around the branch to keep an eye on you.

personality.blurb: Despite the name, the red is on their head. Their black-and-white striped back and loud, rolling kwirr call give them away.

origin: Native woodpeckers who spread north into New York over the past century.
home: On a tree trunk, calling kwirr! across the park.

rightNow.spring: They're calling loudly and carving out a fresh nest hole.
rightNow.summer: They're feeding chicks and snacking on fruit and bugs.
rightNow.fall: They're storing acorns and nuts in cracks in the bark.
rightNow.winter: They're raiding their bark pantries and visiting feeders.

funFact.title: Where's the red belly?
funFact.body: Red-bellied woodpeckers do have a red belly, but it's a faint blush you can barely see. The bright red is on their head.

kindness.title: Keep the old trees.
kindness.body: Big, old trees with a few dead limbs are woodpecker homes. They're worth protecting.

spotHint: Listen for a loud rolling kwirr and look for zebra stripes on a trunk.
withPeople: Red-bellied woodpeckers visit feeders and are loud about it. They'll keep an eye on you but rarely fly far.

personality.blurb: Titmice are small, gray and very curious. Their loud peter-peter-peter whistle rings through the trees all year.

origin: Native songbirds of eastern forests who moved north as parks and yards grew leafy.
home: Hopping through the treetops, whistling peter, peter, peter.

rightNow.spring: They're whistling peter-peter-peter and collecting soft nest lining.
rightNow.summer: They're raising chicks in tree holes and old woodpecker nests.
rightNow.fall: They're joining mixed flocks with chickadees and woodpeckers and stashing seeds.
rightNow.winter: They're leading mixed flocks through the bare trees, cheerful as ever.

funFact.title: Hair for the nest
funFact.body: Titmice line their nests with soft hair, sometimes plucked straight from a sleeping raccoon or a dog.

kindness.title: Leave pet fur out in spring.
kindness.body: Untreated pet fur or cotton tucked in a bush makes great nest lining for titmice.

spotHint: Listen for a loud peter-peter-peter and look for a small gray bird with a pointy crest.
withPeople: Titmice are bold and curious, and will come quite close. They've even been filmed plucking hair from people's heads for their nests.

personality.blurb: Hermit thrushes are shy, spotted birds of the forest floor. Their flute-like song is one of the most beautiful sounds in North America.

origin: Native thrushes who nest in northern forests and pass through, or spend the winter, in our parks.
home: On the leafy ground under the trees, flicking their tail.

rightNow.spring: They're passing through on the way north, sometimes singing a few flute-like notes.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're up in northern forests, filling the woods with song.
rightNow.fall: They're arriving from the north, hopping through the leaf litter in quiet corners.
rightNow.winter: A few are staying all winter, eating berries in the thickets.

funFact.title: A song in harmony
funFact.body: Hermit thrushes sing notes that follow the same harmonic patterns as human music.

kindness.title: Leave the leaves.
kindness.body: Thrushes find their food in leaf litter. A leafy corner under trees is their kitchen.

spotHint: In fall and winter, look in quiet leafy corners for a brown bird with a spotted chest who slowly raises their tail.
withPeople: Hermit thrushes are shy and quiet around people, and slip deeper into the bushes when someone comes along the path.

personality.blurb: Birders call them butter butts for the yellow patch above their tail. They're one of the few warblers tough enough to spend winter here.

origin: Native warblers who nest in northern forests and winter along the coast, including New York.
home: Flitting through the treetops, flashing a yellow rump.

rightNow.spring: They're passing through in big numbers, the males in bright yellow, black and white.
rightNow.summer: Right now they're up north, raising chicks in evergreen forests.
rightNow.fall: They're arriving by the hundreds, and some are staying for the winter.
rightNow.winter: They're eating bayberries and poison ivy berries, flashing that yellow rump.

funFact.title: They can digest wax
funFact.body: Yellow-rumped warblers can digest the waxy coating on bayberries, which lets them survive winters other warblers can't.

kindness.title: Plant bayberry.
kindness.body: Bayberry and other native berry shrubs feed warblers all winter long.

spotHint: Look for a small gray bird with a flash of yellow on the rump, calling check! from the trees.
withPeople: Yellow-rumped warblers mostly ignore people, flitting through the trees overhead, busy with bugs and berries.

personality.blurb: Bumble bees are round, fuzzy and busy from the first warm day to the last. They hum so hard that pollen shakes loose from the flowers.

origin: Native bees of eastern North America, and the most common bumble bee in New York City.
home: Bumbling from flower to flower in the garden beds.

rightNow.spring: Big queens are waking up alone and flying low, searching for a hole to start a nest.
rightNow.summer: Workers are everywhere, legs loaded with orange pollen baskets.
rightNow.fall: New queens are feeding on asters and goldenrod before winter.
rightNow.winter: Only the new queens are left, asleep underground until spring.

funFact.title: Buzz pollination
funFact.body: Bumble bees grab a flower and vibrate their flight muscles so hard that pollen shakes out. Tomatoes love it.

kindness.title: Leave some bare soil.
kindness.body: Bumble bee queens nest in old burrows and messy corners. A wild patch is a nursery.

spotHint: On a warm day, check flowers for a round, fuzzy, black-and-yellow bee, humming loudly.
withPeople: Bumble bees are gentle and very rarely sting, only if they're squeezed or their nest is disturbed. You can watch them up close on a flower.

personality.blurb: Honey bees tell their sisters where the best flowers are by dancing, a little figure-eight that points the way.

origin: Bees from Europe, Africa and Asia, brought to North America in the 1600s. Many live in rooftop hives around the city.
home: Visiting the flower beds, then heading home to a rooftop hive.

rightNow.spring: Hives are growing fast, and some are swarming: thousands of bees moving house together.
rightNow.summer: Foragers are making trip after trip, bringing nectar home for honey.
rightNow.fall: They're gathering the last nectar and getting the hive ready for winter.
rightNow.winter: They're huddled in a warm ball inside the hive, shivering to keep the queen cozy.

funFact.title: The waggle dance
funFact.body: A honey bee's dance tells the others which direction to fly, measured from the sun, and how far to go.

kindness.title: Put out a shallow dish of water.
kindness.body: Add a few pebbles so bees can land and drink safely on hot days.

spotHint: Look on flowers for a slim, golden-brown bee with stripes, moving quickly from bloom to bloom.
withPeople: People have kept honey bees for thousands of years, and New York City has hundreds of rooftop hives. A honey bee on a flower is busy, not looking for trouble.

personality.blurb: Carpenter bees hover right in front of your face to check you out. That's usually a male, and males don't even have stingers.

origin: Native bees of eastern North America who carve their nests in soft, bare wood.
home: Hovering by the old wooden bench, guarding their tunnel.

rightNow.spring: The males are hovering in the air, chasing off anyone who comes near.
rightNow.summer: Mothers are drilling perfectly round tunnels in wood for their young.
rightNow.fall: The new generation is out, sipping nectar before winter.
rightNow.winter: They're tucked inside old wooden tunnels, waiting for warmth.

funFact.title: Bluffing guards
funFact.body: The carpenter bee who dives at you is a male, and males can't sting. He's all bluff.

kindness.title: Leave them a bit of old wood.
kindness.body: A weathered post or untreated scrap of wood gives carpenter bees somewhere to nest that isn't your porch.

spotHint: Look for a big black bee with a shiny bald bottom, hovering by wooden benches, fences and porches.
withPeople: Carpenter bees hover right in front of people to check them out. That's usually a male, and males can't sting.

personality.blurb: On warm June nights, male fireflies fly low and flash a J-shaped swoop of light. Females in the grass flash back when they like what they see.

origin: Native beetles of eastern North America, who spend most of their lives as glowing larvae in damp soil.
home: Blinking slowly over the dark lawn.

rightNow.spring: The larvae are glowing faintly in damp soil, eating slugs and getting ready.
rightNow.summer: They're flashing over lawns and meadows at dusk.
rightNow.fall: The young are growing underground.
rightNow.winter: The larvae are tucked deep in the soil until spring.

funFact.title: Cold light
funFact.body: A firefly's glow is almost pure light with nearly no heat, made by mixing chemicals inside their belly.

kindness.title: Turn off the porch light.
kindness.body: Fireflies talk in flashes. Darker yards and unraked corners make it easier for them to find each other.

spotHint: On a warm summer evening, just after sunset, look low over grass for slow, rising yellow flashes.
withPeople: Fireflies don't mind people, but our lights make it hard for them to see each other's flashes. Dark yards help them find a mate.

personality.blurb: Blue dashers perch on a twig by the water, wings forward, then zip off to snatch a mosquito out of the air. They catch almost everything they chase.

origin: Native dragonflies of North America who start life underwater as nymphs in ponds and marshes.
home: Zipping low over the water, then back to the same perch.

rightNow.spring: The nymphs are crawling up reed stems to split open and become dragonflies.
rightNow.summer: The males are guarding their favorite perches over the water.
rightNow.fall: The last few are hunting on warm afternoons.
rightNow.winter: The nymphs are waiting underwater, eating and growing.

funFact.title: Nearly perfect hunters
funFact.body: Dragonflies catch around 95 percent of the prey they chase, so a blue dasher eats a lot of mosquitoes and other small insects.

kindness.title: Keep ponds clean.
kindness.body: Dragonflies grow up underwater for months. No pesticides near water means more dragonflies.

spotHint: Near ponds and marshes in summer, look for a powder-blue dragonfly perched on a stick, wings tilted forward.
withPeople: Dragonflies aren't afraid of people and sometimes land on a hat or a shoulder to rest. They don't bite or sting.

personality.blurb: Milkweed bugs gather in groups on milkweed pods, wearing bright orange as a warning: we taste terrible.

origin: Native bugs of North America who live on milkweed, like monarch butterflies.
home: Clustered on the milkweed pods in the meadow.

rightNow.spring: The first ones are arriving from the south.
rightNow.summer: They're gathering on milkweed and laying eggs on the pods.
rightNow.fall: Big clusters of all sizes, from tiny red young to grown-ups, are crowding the seed pods.
rightNow.winter: They've gone south, or they're tucked away until spring.

funFact.title: Borrowed poison
funFact.body: They drink milkweed seeds, which are toxic, and store the poison in their bodies so birds learn to leave them alone.

kindness.title: Plant milkweed.
kindness.body: Milkweed feeds monarchs, milkweed bugs, bees and more. One plant is a whole neighborhood.

spotHint: In late summer, check milkweed pods for clusters of bright orange-and-black bugs.
withPeople: Milkweed bugs are harmless to people. Their bright orange is a warning for birds, not for us.

personality.blurb: Sliders stack up on logs to soak up the sun. When anything startles them, they slide into the water, plop, plop, plop.

origin: Turtles from the southern US. Many in city ponds were once pets (red-eared sliders), and now they're settled in.
home: Basking on the log, legs stretched out.

rightNow.spring: They're waking up and climbing onto logs on the first warm days.
rightNow.summer: They're basking in rows, and the mothers are digging nests in sandy soil.
rightNow.fall: They're soaking up the last warm afternoons before winter.
rightNow.winter: They're resting in the mud at the bottom of the pond, barely breathing.

funFact.title: Breathing through their bottom
funFact.body: In winter, sliders rest underwater for months and can take in oxygen through skin near their tail.

kindness.title: Never release pet turtles.
kindness.body: If you can't keep a turtle, find a rescue. And if you see one crossing a road, help them across in the direction they were going.

spotHint: On sunny days, look at logs and rocks in ponds for turtles lined up, basking.
withPeople: Many sliders in city ponds were once pets that people let go. They're shy now and slide into the water if someone gets close to their log.

personality.blurb: Groundhogs spend summer eating clover and dandelions with total focus, then sleep the whole winter away. They whistle when they're alarmed.

origin: Native rodents of eastern North America, actually a big ground squirrel, living in parks and grassy edges around the city.
home: Munching clover on the lawn, close to their burrow.

rightNow.spring: They've just woken up, hungry and looking for a partner.
rightNow.summer: They're eating, eating, eating, and showing the babies where the best clover is.
rightNow.fall: They're getting very round, and soon they'll disappear underground for the winter.
rightNow.winter: They're hibernating in their burrows, hearts beating just a few times a minute.

funFact.title: Champion sleepers
funFact.body: In hibernation a groundhog's heart slows from about 80 beats a minute to as few as 5, and their body cools almost to freezing.

kindness.title: Leave the clover.
kindness.body: A lawn with clover and dandelions feeds groundhogs, rabbits and bees. Keep dogs leashed near burrows.

spotHint: In parks, look on grassy edges for a big brown furry animal sitting up, or munching with their head down.
withPeople: Groundhogs are wary and dash for their burrow when people come close, but in busy parks some get used to walkers and keep munching.

personality.blurb: Orb-weavers spin a fresh round web most evenings, wait in the middle all night, then eat the old silk to make the next one.

origin: A big family of spiders found all over the world. Many live in our gardens, railings and window frames.
home: In the middle of a web on the railing, glistening.

rightNow.spring: Tiny spiderlings are hatching and floating away on silk threads.
rightNow.summer: Their webs are getting bigger every week.
rightNow.fall: It's their biggest season: huge webs everywhere, sparkling with dew at dawn.
rightNow.winter: Their eggs are waiting in silk sacs for spring.

funFact.title: Silk recyclers
funFact.body: Many orb-weavers eat their web before making a new one, recycling the silk protein for the next night.

kindness.title: Walk around the web.
kindness.body: A web takes about an hour to build. If one's in your way, duck under it. The spider will thank you (quietly).

spotHint: In late summer and fall, look for round webs on railings, fences and shrubs, especially at dawn when dew lights them up.
withPeople: Orb-weavers are shy and almost never bite people. They'd much rather wait in their web for a moth.

personality.blurb: Red foxes trot along the edges of the dunes and meadows at dawn and dusk, listening for mice in the grass, then leap up and pounce nose-first.

origin: Native to New York (and found all over the northern half of the world), living in the city's wildest waterfront parks, mostly on Staten Island and around the outer beaches.
home: Along the edges of dunes, meadows and brushy parkland, with a den dug into a sandy bank.

rightNow.spring: Kits are tumbling out of the den, play-fighting while their parents bring home food.
rightNow.summer: The kits are learning to hunt, pouncing on grasshoppers in the tall grass at dusk.
rightNow.fall: This year's young are heading off to find their own patch.
rightNow.winter: They're courting in the snow, and you might hear their eerie barks after dark.

funFact.title: The mouse pounce
funFact.body: A fox can hear a mouse squeak under the snow, then jump high and dive nose-first right on top of them. They seem to aim better when facing northeast.

kindness.title: Watch from far away.
kindness.body: Never feed foxes or leave food out for them. Keep dogs leashed and give dens plenty of room, especially in spring.

spotHint: Look at dawn or dusk along dune trails and meadow edges in the quietest waterfront parks. A flash of orange with a white-tipped tail.
withPeople: Foxes are shy and keep their distance. They may get bold where people feed them, which isn't good for them, so watch quietly and let them be wild.

personality.blurb: Coyotes moved into the city on their own, trotting down rail lines and greenways. They travel at night, keep their distance from people and know every shortcut in the park.

origin: Native to North America, spreading east over the last century. They reached the Bronx in the 1990s and now live in its big parks, with a few wandering farther.
home: In the woods and meadows of the biggest parks, resting in thickets by day.

rightNow.spring: Pups are being born in dens hidden in the thickest corners of the park.
rightNow.summer: Families are out at night, the pups learning to hunt mice and voles.
rightNow.fall: The young are heading out to find their own territory, some traveling a long way.
rightNow.winter: Pairs are courting, and their yips and howls carry across the park on cold nights.

funFact.title: Sneaking into the city
funFact.body: Coyotes reached the Bronx by following highways, rail lines and green corridors south. One even made it across a bridge into Queens.

kindness.title: Let them stay wild.
kindness.body: Never feed coyotes. Keep pets inside at night, put trash away and give any coyote you see plenty of space.

spotHint: Very rarely seen. Early morning or late evening in the biggest Bronx parks, a gray-brown dog with a bushy, black-tipped tail trotting away.
withPeople: Coyotes in the city usually avoid people completely and move at night. The ones that get fed lose their fear, which gets them into trouble.

personality.blurb: As the light goes, little brown bats come out to zigzag over ponds, streetlights and rooftops, catching bugs by listening to the echoes of their own clicks.

origin: Native. Big brown bats live in the city all year, and eastern red bats, hoary bats and others pass through on migration.
home: Tucked into tree hollows, loose bark, attics and cracks in old buildings by day.

rightNow.spring: They're waking up from winter and coming out to hunt on warm evenings.
rightNow.summer: Moms are raising pups in snug roosts, and the sky over the ponds is full of zigzagging bats at dusk.
rightNow.fall: Some are flying south, and the ones who stay are fattening up for a long winter sleep.
rightNow.winter: They're hibernating in cool, quiet spots, barely breathing until spring.

funFact.title: Seeing with sound
funFact.body: Bats make high clicks, too high for us to hear, and listen to the echoes to find a moth in the dark. A single bat can catch hundreds of bugs in an hour.

kindness.title: Turn off a light.
kindness.body: Dark yards and gardens with native flowers bring the moths bats eat. Never touch a bat on the ground: call a wildlife rehabber instead.

spotHint: Right at dusk on warm evenings, look up over ponds, lawns and streetlights for fast, fluttery zigzags.
withPeople: Bats stay out of our way and eat the bugs who bite us. They're gentle, but a bat on the ground may be sick, so never pick one up.

personality.blurb: Cottontails nibble clover at the edges of lawns and freeze perfectly still when anyone comes near. If that doesn't work, they zigzag away, flashing their white tail.

origin: Native rabbits of eastern North America, living in parks, meadows and leafy edges all over the city.
home: On the grassy edges of parks, close to thick bushes they can dash into.

rightNow.spring: Moms are tucking tiny babies into shallow nests in the grass, lined with their own fur.
rightNow.summer: Young rabbits are everywhere, nibbling clover at the edges of the lawns.
rightNow.fall: They're fattening up and growing thick winter coats.
rightNow.winter: They're nibbling twigs and bark, staying close to the thickest bushes.

funFact.title: Hidden in plain sight
funFact.body: A mother cottontail visits her nest only at dawn and dusk, so she doesn't lead anyone to it. Babies alone in the nest are usually just fine.

kindness.title: Leave the nest be.
kindness.body: If you find a nest of baby rabbits, leave it and keep dogs away. Mom is coming back after dark.

spotHint: At dawn and dusk, look along the edges of big lawns, close to bushes, for a small brown rabbit sitting very, very still.
withPeople: Cottontails freeze or zigzag away from people, but in busy parks some get used to walkers and keep munching.

personality.blurb: Wild turkeys stroll through Staten Island yards and parks in big flocks, the males puffing up and fanning their tails, and at night they fly up into tall trees to sleep.

origin: Native. Gone from the area for a long time, they came back and are now a familiar sight on Staten Island and in the big Bronx parks.
home: In flocks on lawns, woods and quiet streets, roosting high in tall trees at night.

rightNow.spring: The males are strutting with their tails fanned and gobbling to impress the hens.
rightNow.summer: Hens are leading little flocks of poults through the tall grass.
rightNow.fall: Big flocks are roaming the parks and yards, scratching for acorns.
rightNow.winter: They're traveling in big flocks, roosting together high in the trees on cold nights.

funFact.title: They can fly
funFact.body: Wild turkeys are strong fliers for short bursts, up to 55 miles an hour, and every night they fly up into tall trees to sleep.

kindness.title: Give them the road.
kindness.body: Drive slowly where turkeys cross, never feed them, and give a puffed-up spring male plenty of room.

spotHint: On Staten Island, look for a flock on a lawn or a quiet street, or listen for gobbling in spring.
withPeople: Most wild turkeys keep their distance, but where people feed them they can get bold, and spring males sometimes puff up at walkers. Give them space and they'll go about their business.
